title: Given an unsorted array of numbers, find the K numbers that appear most frequently. Explain how a frequency map plus a min-heap keyed on frequency finds them efficiently.
shortTitle: Top K Frequent Numbers (Find the K Most Frequently Occurring Numbers)

s1_definition.profdef: Top K Frequent Numbers is a Top K Elements problem combined with frequency counting. We first count occurrences of each number into a hash map, then keep a min-heap of size K ordered by frequency. Each distinct number is offered to the heap; when the heap exceeds K we evict the least frequent. The heap ends with the K most frequent numbers, giving O(n plus d log K) time where d is the number of distinct values.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, we want the K merchant categories that Rajesh spends on most often. We first tally how many times each category appears, then keep a small bucket of the K most frequent categories, where the least frequent kept category sits on top so a more frequent one can push it out.
s1_definition.oneliner: Count frequencies in a map, then keep a size-K min-heap keyed on frequency, evicting the least frequent when the heap overflows.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Top K Frequent Numbers is a Top K Elements problem combined with frequency counting. We first count occurrences of each number into a hash map, then keep a min-heap of size K ordered by frequency. Each distinct number is offered to the heap; when the heap exceeds K we evict the least frequent. The heap ends with the K most frequent numbers, giving O(n plus d log K) time where d is the number of distinct values.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, we want the K merchant categories that Rajesh spends on most often. We first tally how many times each category appears, then keep a small bucket of the K most frequent categories, where the least frequent kept category sits on top so a more frequent one can push it out.

**One line to remember:** Count frequencies in a map, then keep a size-K min-heap keyed on frequency, evicting the least frequent when the heap overflows.

sections.s2_technical:
We build a frequency map with `map.merge(num, 1, Integer::sum)` for each number, counting occurrences in O(n). Then we create a min-heap ordered by the map's frequency values: `PriorityQueue<Integer> minHeap = new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> map.get(a) - map.get(b));`. We iterate over the distinct keys, offering each; whenever the heap size exceeds K we poll, which removes the least frequent kept number. For example, `minHeap.offer(key); if (minHeap.size() > K) minHeap.poll();`.

After processing all distinct keys, the heap holds the K numbers with the highest frequencies. Ordering the heap by frequency with the root being the least frequent is what lets the overflow eviction drop exactly the weakest candidate each time.

A senior nuance is that when K approaches the number of distinct values, a bucket sort by frequency, placing numbers into buckets indexed by their count and reading from the high end, gives O(n) time, which beats the heap's O(n plus d log K); mentioning both shows range. Another nuance is that ties in frequency are broken arbitrarily unless the problem specifies otherwise. Complexity is O(n plus d log K) time and O(n) space.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India wants the K merchant categories that a customer like Rajesh transacts in most frequently, for a rewards recommendation, from a long transaction history. This is exactly how Top K Frequent Numbers works.

Problem 2 — Sorting all categories by frequency is more work than needed when only K are wanted. This is why we count frequencies once and keep a size-K min-heap keyed on frequency, evicting the least frequent kept category whenever a more frequent one arrives.

The code defines a `SpendPatternService` exposing `topKFrequent(categoryIds, k)` returning the K most frequent category ids. A `Demo` finds the top two categories and logs them.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: categories 10, 10, 20, 30, 20, 10, 40, 20 and K equal to 2.

Step 1: Count frequencies: category 10 appears three times, category 20 appears three times, category 30 once, category 40 once.

Step 2: Offer category 10 to the heap, size one. Offer category 20, size two, still within K.

Step 3: Offer category 30 with frequency one; heap size is three, exceeding K, so poll the least frequent, which is category 30, dropping it.

Step 4: Offer category 40 with frequency one; heap size is three again, so poll the least frequent kept, dropping category 40.

Step 5: The heap holds categories 10 and 20, each with frequency three, the two most frequent.

```
Oct 28, 2026 12:34:52 AM com.bank.spend.service.SpendPatternService topKFrequent
INFO: Top 2 frequent categories = [20, 10] freq={10=3, 20=3, 30=1, 40=1}
INFO: Rajesh SAV2001 top 2 categories: [20, 10]
```


sections.s6_takeaway:
Top K Frequent Numbers blends frequency counting with the Top K Elements pattern. I first pass over the array once and count how many times each number occurs into a hash map. Then I keep a min-heap of size K, but crucially the heap is ordered by frequency rather than by the numbers themselves, so its root is the least frequent of the numbers I am currently keeping.

I iterate over the distinct numbers, offering each into the heap, and whenever the heap grows beyond K I poll the root, which removes the least frequent kept number. That overflow-then-evict step guarantees I always discard the weakest candidate, so when I have processed every distinct number the heap holds exactly the K most frequent ones. The counting is linear, and the heap work is the number of distinct values times the logarithm of K.

At the National Bank of India I used this to find the K merchant categories a customer like Rajesh transacts in most often, powering a rewards recommendation from a long transaction history. I counted category frequencies once and kept a size-K min-heap keyed on frequency, evicting the least frequent kept category whenever a more frequent one arrived. I would also mention that when K is close to the number of distinct values, a bucket sort by frequency achieves linear time, which shows an interviewer I know when to switch tools.
